Surah 41, Verses 1–4

Makkan, and its number of verses is 54, though it is said 53. [It was revealed after Ghafir.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

If you make Ha-Mim the name of the surah, it is in the position of the subject (mubtada'), and tanzil (revelation) is its predicate. If you make it an enumeration of the letters, then tanzil is the predicate of an omitted subject, and kitab is a substitute (badal) for tanzil, or a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj permitted that tanzil be the subject and kitab its predicate.

Its justification is that tanzil is specified by the following description, so it was permissible for it to occur as a subject. fussilat ayatuhu: its verses were distinguished and made into detailed elements with different meanings: rulings, parables, admonitions, promise and threat, and other things. It is also read fussilat, meaning: they were distinguished between truth and falsehood. Or some of them were separated from others by the variation of their meanings, from your saying "fassala min al-balad" (he departed from the town).

Qur'anan 'arabiyyan (an Arabic Qur'an) is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas) and praise, meaning: by this detailed book is intended a Qur'an whose attributes are such and such. It is also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: its verses were detailed while it was an Arabic Qur'an.

li-qawmin ya'lamun (for a people who know): that is, for an Arab people who know what was revealed to them of the detailed verses, explained in their clear Arabic tongue, so that nothing in it is obscure to them.

If you ask: to what does the phrase li-qawmin ya'lamun relate?

I say: it may relate to tanzil or to fussilat, meaning: a revelation from Allah for their sake, or its verses were detailed for them.

The better view is that it is a description, like what precedes and what follows it, meaning: an Arabic Qur'an existing for an Arab people, so that the relative clauses and descriptions are not separated.

It is also read bashiran wa-nadhiran (as a bringer of glad tidings and a warner), as a description of the book, or as the predicate of an omitted subject.

fa-hum la yasma'un (but most of them do not hear): they do not accept and do not obey. It is like your saying, "I interceded with so-and-so but he did not hear my words," though he did hear them, but since he did not accept them and did not act upon their requirement, it is as if he had not heard them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verse 5:

Al-akinna (ۘthe coverings): plural of kinan, which is a covering. Al-waqr, with a fatha on the waw, means heaviness. It has also been read with a kasra. These are figurative expressions for the impenetrability of their hearts to accepting and believing in the truth, as if they were in wrappings and coverings that prevent it from penetrating them, like His saying ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in wrappings"﴾, and the deafness of their ears to it, as if there were deafness in them toward it. And because the two ways and the two religions are far apart, it is as if between them and what they are upon, and between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and what he is upon, there were a concealing barrier and an impregnable obstacle, like a mountain or something similar, so they neither meet nor see each other. ﴿So act upon your religion; indeed we are acting upon ours.﴾ Or: act in nullifying our affair; indeed we are acting in nullifying yours. It has also been read: "innā ʿāmilūn" (inna ʿamilun). If you ask: Is there any benefit in the addition of min in His saying ﴿and between us and you there is a barrier﴾? I say: Yes, because if it were said, "and between us and you a barrier," the meaning would be that a barrier exists in the middle of the two directions. But with the addition of min, the meaning is that a barrier begins from us and begins from you, so the intermediate distance between our direction and your direction is filled entirely with the barrier, with no empty space in it.

[Mahmud said: "If you ask: What is the benefit of min in His saying ﴿and between us and you there is a barrier﴾? He answered that its benefit is to indicate that the barrier begins from their side, and also begins from his side, so it follows that the intermediate distance between them is filled with the barrier, with no empty space in it. Without mentioning min there, the meaning would be: that in the distance between them there is only a barrier." Ahmad said: The meaning is not altered by the entry of min from what it was before. If it were as he mentioned, then min would have to be understood with the second bayn, since he made it indicate the beginning in the second just as it indicates the beginning in the first. The implied sense would then be: "and from between us and between you a barrier." This clearly disturbs the meaning of bayn, because it refuses the repetition of its governing word with it. Even if a speaker said, "I sat between Zayd, and I sat between ʿAmr," it would not be correct, because repeating the governing word makes bayn govern a single noun only, cutting it off from its preceding companion. Its nature is to govern a plural, because within its meaning is the notion of being in the middle. Al-Zamakhshari went further and made the second bayn different from the first, because he took the first to be on their side and the second on his side. The matter is not as he supposed. Rather, the first bayn is the very same as the second, and it expresses the intermediate direction between the two things joined. Its repetition was only because the conjoined element is an elided, preserved element, so its preserver, which is bayn, must be repeated. The proof of this is that there is no disagreement that there is no difference between saying "I sat between Zayd and ʿAmr" and saying "I sat between Zayd and between ʿAmr." Its repetition with a noun is permissible, while with a pronoun it is obligatory, for the reason we have explained. When this is clear, the apparent meaning, and God knows best, is that the position of min here is like its position in His saying ﴿And We have set before them a barrier and behind them a barrier﴾, to indicate that the intermediate direction between them and the Prophet, peace be upon him, is merely the beginning of the barrier, and that its presence is close to its absence. Do you not see that at the end of this verse, min is not used in it, namely His saying ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier. And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾? The words of al-Zamakhshari, when you test them by the verification we have mentioned, show their weakness, and God is the Granter of success. In this verse and its counterpart there is an intensity of expression and eloquence that is not fitting to be arranged except among the pearls of the Noble Book, for they include mention of three successive barriers, each of which is sufficient in its own domain. The first is the external barrier intervening; next is the barrier of deafness; and the furthest is the barrier that covers the heart, and we seek refuge in Allah. This verse leaves no loosened barrier without letting it down, and leaves these wretched people no hope and no outcry without seizing it. So we ask Allah for His sufficiency.]

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verses 6–7:**

If you ask: from where does His saying ﴿Indeed, I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me﴾ come as an answer to their saying ﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, how is this an answer to what precedes it?" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: He answered with what we summarize as follows. When they refused to accept from him, peace be upon him, in every way, he began by establishing the proof that acceptance of him is obligatory, for he is a human being like them, with no power to display the miracles that have appeared. Rather, the only one able to display them is God Most High, as confirmation of him, peace be upon him. Then, after the proof was established against them, he explained to them the most important thing he was sent with, which is monotheism (tawhid), and within steadfastness are included all the details of the Law (shar'). He completed this by warning them against refusing acceptance, with a lengthy punishment (al-wayl al-tawil).]]? I say: from the fact that he said to them: I am not an angel; I am only a human being like you, and it has been revealed to me apart from you. So by the revelation to me, while I am a human being, my prophethood is established; and when my prophethood is established, you are obliged to follow me. And in what is revealed to me is that your God is one God, ﴿so go straight to Him﴾, that is, be upright toward Him through monotheism and sincerity in worship, not veering to the right or to the left, and not turning to what Satan adorns for you of taking allies and intercessors. ﴿And seek His forgiveness﴾, repent to Him of the polytheism that has preceded for you. It is also read: "He said, 'Indeed, I am only a human being.'"

If you ask: why did He single out, among the attributes of the polytheists, the withholding of zakat, paired with disbelief in the Hereafter? I say:

Because the thing most beloved to a person is his wealth, and it is the twin of his soul. So when he spends it in God's cause, that is the strongest evidence of his steadfastness, his truthfulness of intention, and the purity of his inner disposition. Do you not see His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and as a strengthening of their own souls﴾ (2:265), meaning: they make their souls firm and show their firmness by spending wealth. The "ones whose hearts are to be reconciled" (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum) were only tempted by a morsel (lamzah) of this world, [[His saying "only by a morsel of the world": in al-Sihah (a lexicon), "lamaza" means that one follows the remnant of food in the mouth with the tongue. So "lamzah" means "malmuzah" (what is licked), as "mudghah" means "mamdughah" (what is chewed). (Ea.)]] so their zealotry was subdued and their stubbornness softened. And the apostates (ahl al-riddah) after the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, only openly displayed opposition by withholding zakat, so war was declared against them and they were fought.

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask, why did he single out zakat? He answered that the thing most beloved to a person is his wealth, and it is the twin of his soul, so giving it up is the proof of his steadfastness and the purity of his inner disposition. The ones whose hearts are to be reconciled were only tempted by a morsel of this world, and the apostates only displayed opposition by withholding zakat, so war was declared against them and they were fought." Ahmad said: It is a fine statement after changing his words "the ones whose hearts..." to "were tempted," for using the word "deceived" (khada'a) is not fitting, since the Prophet, peace be upon him, reconciled them to faith out of gentleness, repelling evil with good, and what is of this kind.]]

In it there is an incitement of the believers to pay zakat and a severe warning against withholding it, since withholding has been made one of the attributes of the polytheists and is paired with disbelief in the Hereafter. It was also said: the Quraysh used to feed the pilgrims while preventing whoever among them believed in the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, [from doing so]. It was also said: they do not do what would make them pure (azkiya'), which is faith.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 41, verses 9–12:**

﴿أَإِنَّكُمْ﴾ with two hamzas [[Editor's note: his words "أإنكم بهمزتين" perhaps mean: it is recited with two hamzas... etc. (ʿ)]]: the second is pronounced between hamza and the vowel (bayna bayn). ﴿وَءَائِنَّكُمْ﴾ with an alif between two hamzas. ﴿ذَلِكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ الْأَرْضَ فِي يَوْمَيْنِ﴾ "That is He who created the earth in the span of two days." ﴿هُوَ رَبُّ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ "He is the Lord of the worlds." ﴿رَوَاسِيَ﴾ means mountains, firm and fixed.

If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿مِنْ فَوْقِهَا﴾ ("from above it")? Was it abbreviated to His saying ﴿وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا رَوَاسِيَ﴾ ("and He placed in it firm mountains"), like His other sayings ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا فِيهَا رَوَاسِيَ شَامِخَاتٍ﴾ ("and We placed in it towering firm mountains"), ﴿وَجَعَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ رَوَاسِيَ﴾ ("and We placed firm mountains in the earth"), and ﴿وَجَعَلَ لَهَا رَوَاسِيَ﴾ ("and He placed for it firm mountains")? I answer: if they were beneath it like pillars on which it rests, or fixed in it like nails, they would also prevent it from shaking. He chose to set them above the earth so that the benefits in the mountains would be exposed to those who seek them, present to those who gather them, and so that one would see that the earth and the mountains are burdens upon burdens, all in need of a holder that they cannot do without, and He is the One who holds them, mighty and exalted, by His power.

﴿وَبَارَكَ فِيهَا﴾ "and He blessed in it," meaning He increased its good and made it grow. ﴿وَقَدَّرَ فِيهَا أَقْوَاتَهَا﴾ "and measured in it its sustenance," meaning the provisions of its people, their livelihoods, and whatever suits them.

In the reading of Ibn Masʿud: ﴿وَقَسَمَ فِيهَا أَقْوَاتَهَا﴾ "and divided in it its sustenance." ﴿فِي أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍ سَوَاءً﴾ "in four days, equal" is a summation (fadhlaka) of the duration of God's creating the earth and what is in it, as if He said: all of that was in four complete days, equal, without increase or decrease. It was said: God created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and what is in it on Tuesday and Wednesday. Al-Zajjaj said: "in four days" means "in the completion of four days," intending by the completion the two days.

"Equal" (sawaʾan) is read with three vowels: the genitive, as a description; the accusative, as in "it became equal" (istawat sawaʾan), meaning "equality"; and the nominative, as in "it is equal" (hiya sawaʾ).

If you ask: to what does ﴿لِلسَّائِلِينَ﴾ "for those who ask" relate? I answer: it relates to an omitted element, as if it were said: this limitation is for the sake of the one who asked, "In how many days was the earth and what is in it created?" Or it may be taken as: "He measured in it its sustenance for those who seek it, who need it, the eaters."

[The following is the commentator's (Ibn al-Munayyir's) critique of al-Zamakhshari's text, as it appears in the source.]

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The statement ﴿فِي أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍ﴾ is a summation of the duration of God's creating the earth and what is in it; as if He said: and He measured in it its sustenance in two other days, so that makes four days equal. Its meaning, 'equal,' is: complete, balanced, without increase or decrease." He quoted from al-Zajjaj that the meaning of the verse is "in the completion of four days," intending by the completion the two days. Then he said: "If you ask, to what does ﴿لِلسَّائِلِينَ﴾ relate? He answered that it relates to an omitted element, as if it were said: this limitation is for the sake of the one who asked, 'In how many days was the earth and what is in it created?' Or it is to be estimated: that is, He measured in it the sustenance for those seeking it who need it, the eaters. Then he said: 'This last aspect is only consistent with al-Zajjaj's interpretation.'"

Ahmad said: He did not explain its inconsistency with the first interpretation, so we will explain it. The requirement of the first interpretation is that ﴿فِي أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍ﴾ is a summation, and such a summation naturally occurs at the end of a speech after it is complete. So if ﴿لِلسَّائِلِينَ﴾ were made to relate to an estimated element, the summation would fall in the middle of the speech. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verse 13–14:

So if they turn away after you recite to them these proofs of His oneness and power, then warn them of a thunderbolt (ṣāʿiqa): that is, a punishment of severe impact, as if it were a thunderbolt. It has been read as ṣaʿqa, like the ṣaʿqa of ʿĀd and Thamūd: this is the single instance of the verb ṣaʿaqa (to be struck), and it is either ṣaʿqa or ṣuʿqa. One says: "The thunderbolt struck him (ṣaʿaqathu al-ṣāʿiqa ṣaʿqan), so he was struck (faṣuʿiqa ṣaʿqan)," and this is of the pattern of: "I did it, so he did it" (faʿaltuhu fafaʿala).

"From before them and from behind them" means: they came to them from every side, exerted themselves with them, and employed every stratagem against them, yet they saw from them nothing but obstinacy and aversion. ﴿And the Word has come due against them﴾, meaning the word of punishment, ﴿among nations﴾, in the company of nations. Similar to this is what is in His saying:

The pronoun refers to them and to the nations.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verses 26–28:

It has been read: "wa-lghaw fihi" (وَالْغَوْا فِيهِ), with the ghayn both fathah and dammah. It is said: laghā yalghā, and laghā yalghū. Al-laghw (لغو) is the discourse that falls away, having no benefit in it. It is said: "min al-lughā wa-rafath al-takallum" (from the idle talk and the obscene speech). The meaning is: do not listen to it when it is recited, and occupy yourselves, when it is recited, with raising the voices in nonsense, babble, and "al-zamal" [[His words "al-zamal," which in the Sihah is "al-azmal," meaning the cry; and "al-azmula" (with a damma) means the one who cries out among wild goats and others. (Ea.)]] and the like, until you confuse the reciter, disturb him, and overpower him in his recitation. The Quraysh used to instruct one another to do this. "Fa-lanudhiqanna alladhina kafaru" (So We shall surely make those who disbelieved taste...): it is permissible that by "those who disbelieved" is meant these idle talkers and those who command them to idle talk specifically, and that "those who disbelieved" is mentioned generally so that they are included under that mention. We have already mentioned the addition of "asw'a" (worst) in a way that suffices without repeating it. From Ibn Abbas: "adhaban shadidan" (a severe punishment) refers to the Battle of Badr. "Aswa'a alladhi kanu ya'malun" (the worst of what they used to do) — in the Hereafter. "Dhalika" (that) is a reference to the worst; and it must be that the estimate is: the worst reward of those who used to do, so that this reference is correct. "Al-nar" (the Fire) is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) for the recompense, or the predicate of an omitted subject.

If you say: what is the meaning of His words, "lahum fīhā dāru al-khuld" (for them therein is the abode of eternity)? I say: its meaning is that the Fire itself is the abode of eternity, like His words, "Indeed, you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example" (Q. 33:21), meaning that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is an excellent example. And you say, "For you in this house is the house of joy," while you mean the very house itself. "Jazā'an bimā kānū bi-āyātinā yajhadūn" (a recompense for what they used to deny Our signs): that is, a recompense for what they used to babble in it, so He mentioned the denial, which is the cause of the idle talk.

The meaning is: do not listen to it when it is recited, and occupy yourselves, when it is recited, with raising the voices in nonsense, babble, and "al-zamal" [[His words "al-zamal," which in the Sihah is "al-azmal," meaning the cry; and "al-azmula" (with a damma) means the one who cries out among wild goats and others. (Ea.)]] and the like, until you confuse the reciter, disturb him, and overpower him in his recitation. The Quraysh used to instruct one another to do this. "Fa-lanudhiqanna alladhina kafaru" (So We shall surely make those who disbelieved taste...): it is permissible that by "those who disbelieved" is meant these idle talkers and those who command them to idle talk specifically, and that "those who disbelieved" is mentioned generally so that they are included under that mention. We have already mentioned the addition of "asw'a" (worst) in a way that suffices without repeating it. From Ibn Abbas: "adhaban shadidan" (a severe punishment) refers to the Battle of Badr. "Aswa'a alladhi kanu ya'malun" (the worst of what they used to do) — in the Hereafter. "Dhalika" (that) is a reference to the worst; and it must be that the estimate is: the worst reward of those who used to do, so that this reference is correct. "Al-nar" (the Fire) is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) for the recompense, or the predicate of an omitted subject.

If you say: what is the meaning of His words, "lahum fīhā dāru al-khuld" (for them therein is the abode of eternity)? I say: its meaning is that the Fire itself is the abode of eternity, like His words, "Indeed, you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example" (Q. 33:21), meaning that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is an excellent example. And you say, "For you in this house is the house of joy," while you mean the very house itself. "Jazā'an bimā kānū bi-āyātinā yajhadūn" (a recompense for what they used to deny Our signs): that is, a recompense for what they used to babble in it, so He mentioned the denial, which is the cause of the idle talk.

Those who led us astray: i.e., the two devils who led us astray, of the jinn and of mankind. For the devil is of two kinds: a jinn devil and a human devil. God the Exalted says: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and jinn﴾ [al-An'am 6:112], and He the Exalted says: ﴿who whispers in the breasts of mankind, of the jinn and of mankind﴾ [al-Nas 114:5-6]. It is also said: they are Iblis and Qabil, because they initiated disbelief and killing without right.

It is read: "arina" (with a sukun on the ra'), to lighten the kasra, just as they say "fakhd" for "fakhid" (thigh).

It is also said: its meaning is "a'tina" (give us), that is, give to those who led us astray. They related from al-Khalil that when you say "arini thawbaka" with a kasra, the meaning is "baṣṣirnīhi" (show me it), and when you say it with a sukun, it is a request for giving (ista'taa'), meaning "a'tini thawbaka" (give me your garment). Its parallel is the common use of "al-itaa'" (giving) in the sense of "al-i'taa'" (giving). Its original sense is "al-ihdaar" (bringing into presence).

Then (the steadfastness is mentioned after the affirmation, indicating its later rank), and its superiority over it, because steadfastness carries all the importance. A similar expression is His saying, ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then have not doubted﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:15]. The meaning is: they remained firm upon the affirmation and its requirements.

It is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him): "They were steadfast in deed as they were steadfast in word."

And from him: that he recited it and then said, "What do you say about it?" They said, "They did not commit sins." He said, "You have taken the matter to its extreme." They said, "Then what do you say?" He said, "They did not return to worshipping idols."

And from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "They remained upon the path, not swerving like the swerving of foxes."

And from Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him): "They made their deeds sincere."

And from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "They performed the obligatory duties."

Sufyan ibn Abd Allah al-Thaqafi (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, tell me a matter to hold fast to.' He said, 'Say: My Lord is Allah, then be steadfast.' I said, 'What is the thing you fear most for me?' Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took hold of his own tongue and said, 'This.'" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ahmad and Ibn Hibban in full; its origin is in Muslim.]

﴿The angels descend upon them﴾ at the time of death, with good tidings.

It is said that the good tidings are in three places: at death, in the grave, and when they rise from their graves.

﴿That do not fear﴾: here "an" (أَلَّا) is in the sense of "ay" (أي), or it is the light form of the heavy (an). Its origin is "bi-annahu la takhafu," and the "ha'" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "la takhafu," meaning they say, "Do not fear."

Fear (al-khawf) is distress that befalls one due to the anticipation of something disliked, and grief (al-huzn) is distress that befalls one due to its occurrence, from the loss of a benefit or the attainment of harm. The meaning is: Allah has decreed for you security from every distress, so you will never taste it. It is also said: "Do not fear what you are about to face, and do not grieve over what you have left behind." Just as the devils are the companions and brothers of the disobedient, so too the angels are the allies and beloved of the God-fearing in both abodes.

﴿And you shall have what you desire﴾: that is, what you wish for.

"Nuzul" (النزل) means the provision of a guest (al-nazil), who is the visitor, and its accusative case is as a circumstantial state (hal).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verse 33:

Who calls to Allah. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who called to Islam and did righteous deeds in what lies between him and his Lord, and made Islam his creed (nihla) for himself. And from him: they are the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And ʿAisha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: we did not doubt that this verse was revealed concerning the muezzins (al-muʾadhdhinun). It is general in its application to everyone who combines these three things: that he is a monotheist (muwahhid) adhering to the religion of Islam, acting righteously and calling to it. They are none other than the class of learned people who act, from among the people of justice and monotheism, the callers to the religion of Allah. [[His statement "the people of justice and monotheism, the learned who act, the callers" — if by them he means the Muʿtazila, they named themselves thus, so there is no basis for restricting it.(ʿ)]] As for his words "And he says: Indeed I am of the Muslims," the purpose is not that he uttered this speech, but that he made the religion of Islam his doctrine and belief, just as you say: "This is the view of Abu Hanifa," meaning his school of thought.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verses 34–35:

It means that the good deed and the evil deed differ in themselves. So take hold of the good deed that is better than its counterpart, when two good deeds confront you, and repel with it the evil that comes to you from some of your enemies. An example of this: a man wrongs you with a wrong, so the good deed is that you pardon him, and the one that is better is that you do good to him in return for his wronging you, such as when he reviles you and you praise him, or when he kills your son and you ransom his son from the hand of his enemy. For when you do that, your bitter enemy becomes like a close friend, devoted to you. Then he said: "None receives this disposition, or this natural quality, which is returning evil with good, except people of patience, and none but a man of great good fortune who has been granted a great share of good."

If you ask: "Why was it not said: repel with that which is better?" I answer: it is on the presumption of a speaker who said: "How shall I act?" So it was said: "Repel with that which is better." It is also said that "lā" is superfluous, and the meaning is: "The good deed and the evil deed are not equal." If you ask: "On this interpretation, the analogy would have been to say: repel with that which is a good deed," I answer: Yes, but "that which is better" was placed in the position of "the good deed" so that it would be more emphatic in repelling by means of good, because whoever repels with the best finds it easy to repel with what is lower than it.

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "With that which is better" means patience at anger, forbearance at ignorance, and pardon at wrongdoing. And "the share" was interpreted as reward. From al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him: "By Allah, no share is greater than Paradise." It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who was a hostile enemy harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then became a devoted friend.

The word *nazgh* and *nasgh* have the same meaning, and it is like a prick (*nakhs*). The Shaytan "pricks" (*yanzagh*) a person, as if he pricks him, by urging him toward what is not fitting. The *nazgh* is made the one who pricks (*nazigh*), as is said: *jadd jaddahu* (a more intensive form of the same root). Or the intended meaning is: "And if a pricker (*nazigh*) pricks you," describing the Shaytan with the verbal noun. Or it is for its enticement (*taswil*). The meaning is: "And if Shaytan turns you away from what you were enjoined, namely repelling evil with what is better, ﴿then seek refuge in Allah﴾ from his evil, and proceed in your affair and do not obey him."

The pronoun in "khalaqahunna" (He created them) refers to the night, the day, the sun and the moon, because the rule for a plural of non-rational things is that it takes the feminine singular or feminine plural. It is said: "al-aqlam baraytuha wa baraytuhunna" (the pens, I sharpened it and I sharpened them). Or, since He said "wa min ayatihi" (and among His signs), the word "kunna" is taken in the sense of "ayat" (signs), so it was said: "khalaqahunna" (He created them).

If it is asked: where is the place of prostration? The answer: according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is at "ta'buduna" (you worship), and this is the narration of Masruq from Abdullah, since the word "sajda" (prostration) was mentioned before it. According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, it is at "yas'amun" (they do not tire), because it completes the meaning. This is also reported from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

Perhaps some people among them used to prostrate to the sun and the moon, like the Sabians in their worship of the stars, and they claimed that by prostrating to them they intended prostration to Allah. So they were forbidden this intermediary, and were commanded to direct their prostration to the Face of Allah alone, sincerely, if it is Him they worship and if they were monotheists, not polytheists.

﴿So if they are arrogant﴾, and do not comply with what they were commanded and refuse except the intermediary, then leave them to themselves, for Allah, mighty is His authority, never lacks a worshipper or a prostrator in sincerity. He has the near-stationed servants who glorify Him by night and by day above rivals. His saying ﴿with your Lord﴾ is an expression of nearness, rank and honour.

It is also read: "la yas'amun" (they do not tire), with a kasra on the ya.

Al-Khushū' (humility, submission): abasement and lowliness. It is borrowed for the state of the earth when it is barren, with no vegetation in it. Likewise the earth is described as dormant (hamidah) in His words, Exalted is He, "And you see the earth barren (hamidah)," which is the opposite of its being described as stirring and swelling (al-ihtizaz wa'l-rabw), which is the swelling up: when it becomes fertile and adorned with vegetation, as if it were like the one who struts in his finery, whereas before that it was like the abased, dejected one in tattered rags.

[[The saying "in tattered rags": in al-Sihah, "al-tamr" is a torn garment, and its plural is "al-atmar." (Gh.)]]

It is also read "wa-rabat," meaning it rose up, because when the plant is about to emerge, the earth rises up for it.

It is said: "alhada al-hafir" and "lahada," when he deviated from the straight course; he dug in a side-niche, so the term was borrowed for deviation in interpreting the verses of the Qur'an away from the direction of soundness and rectitude. It is recited as yulhidun and yalhidun, according to the two dialects. And His saying, ﴿they are not hidden from Us﴾, is a threat to them for distortion.

To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. That is: when it is asked about, it is said, "Allah knows." Or: none knows it but Allah.

It was also read: "min thamarat min akmamihinna" (from fruits out of their sheaths). [[The author's words "and it was read: min thamarat min akmamihinna" indicate that the well-known reading is: min thamarat min akmamiha, and the one in al-Nasafi is: min thamarat min akmamiha, and min thamarati min akmamiha. As for "min thamarat min akmamihinna," it is the one with the extra particle here, so verify. (Ghayb)]]. The kumm (kimm), with a kasra on the kaf, is the sheath of the fruit, like the spathe of the palm blossom. That is: no fruit emerges, no female conceives, and no one gives birth except that He knows it. He knows the number of days of the pregnancy, its hours, and its circumstances: whether it is premature (khada', i.e. deficient) or complete, whether male or female, beautiful or ugly, and other things.

﴿Where are My partners?﴾ He attributed them to Himself according to their claim. Its explanation is in His saying, ﴿Where are My partners whom you used to claim?﴾ (16:27). In it is mockery and reproach.

﴿We have informed You﴾, that is, we have made You aware, ﴿that none of us is a witness﴾, that is: none of us today—though we have seen and heard—bears witness that they are Your partners. That is: none of us but is one who affirms Your oneness. Or: none of us sees them, because they have strayed from them, and their gods have strayed from them; they do not perceive them at the moment of rebuke. It was also said: this is the speech of the partners, that is: none of us is a witness testifying to what they attributed to us of partnership. The meaning of their straying from them on this interpretation is that they do not benefit them, so it is as if they strayed from them. ﴿And they thought﴾ and were certain. The maḥīṣ (refuge) is the place of escape.

If you say: "We have informed You" is a report of an announcement that had occurred from them; since they had announced it, why are they asked? I say: it is permissible that "Where are My partners?" be repeated to them as a rebuke, and its repetition in the Qur'an in the form of narration is evidence of the repetition of what is narrated.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: You now know from our hearts and beliefs that we will not bear that false testimony, for when He knows it from their souls, it is as if they had informed Him of it. And it is permissible that it be an inception of announcement and not a report of an announcement that had occurred, as you say: "I informed the king that the matter was such and such."

The word ʿarḍ (breadth, width), which belongs to the attributes of bodies, is used figuratively for the abundance and persistence of supplication, and ṭūl (length) is likewise used for it, just as ghilaẓ (thickness) is used for the severity of punishment.

It is also read as ﴿wa-nāʾa bi-jānibih﴾ with the alif inclined (imālah, a vowel shift toward i) and the nūn vowelled with a kasra for ittibāʿ (vowel harmonization, assimilating a vowel to the one following it). It may also be read as wa-nāʾa, with metathesis (qalb, transposition of letters), as they say rāʾ for ra'y (opinion).

If you ask: clarify for me the meaning of God's words ﴿and turns away, withdrawing his side﴾? I answer: there are two possibilities. The first is that "his side" is placed in the position of "himself," since the place of a thing and its direction are treated as the thing itself, as I mentioned concerning His words ﴿over what I neglected concerning God's side﴾ (39:56). From this is the verse:

"...and I drove away from it
the station of the wolf..."

And a water which I came to for the sake of Arwā,
upon which birds gather like silver leaves,

I startled the sand grouse by it, and drove away from it
the station of the wolf, like a cursed man.

By al-Shammākh. Arwā is the name of his beloved. Al-lujayn (silver) with a fatḥah on the lām and a kasrah on the jīm is what falls from the leaves of the tree, from al-lajn, which is pounding, because the wind or the herdsman strikes it and it falls from the tree. Dhaʿarat, with two fatḥahs, means: she frightened the sand grouse at it, and he singled them out because they are the first birds to reach water. Maqām al-dhīb means its station or its place, and he expressed it this way as a metonymy for the wolf itself, singling it out because the wolf generally comes to water at night.

Al-rajul al-laʿīn is the scarecrow figure set up in the middle of a field in the shape of a man, to drive away vermin. He says: many a water have I come to for the sake of my beloved, hoping she would come to it and I would see her. It is also narrated as "for the sake of meeting Arwā," which suggests it was a meeting place between them. He likens the birds around the water to tree leaves falling in their turbidity, abundance and scattering, and this indicates that he did not come to it often, so it is suitable as a meeting place for union. "Dhaʿarat..." to the end is a metonymy for his coming at night. "Like a cursed man" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) referring either to the pronoun of the poet, meaning that he outpaced the sand grouse and the wolf and sat there, or to the wolf, meaning in a frightening state. This contains evidence of the poet's courage and boldness.

That is, "and I drove the wolf away from it." From this is the verse ﴿and for one who fears the station of his Lord﴾ (55:46). And from this is the expression of letter-writers: "I attended Fulān and his assembly," and "I wrote to his direction and to his noble side," meaning himself and his person. So it is as if He said: "and turned away with himself," like the saying about the arrogant man: "he went off with himself," "pride carried him off in every direction," and "conceit blew him about." And "his side" may be understood as his flank, and it is then an expression for deviation and turning aside, as they say: "he bent his flank" and "he turned away with his shoulder."

"Tell me" (أَرَأَيْتُمْ): (say:) Tell me, if the Qur'an is from God (﴿If the Qur'an is from God﴾)—meaning: what you hold, namely your denial of the Qur'an and your rejection of it, is not a matter issuing from a decisive proof by which you attained certainty and the breast was set at rest. Rather, before examining and following the evidence, it is a matter of possibility: it may be from God, and it may not be from Him. You have not reflected or investigated, so what prevents you from acknowledging that it may be the truth while you have disbelieved in it? Then tell me: who is more astray than you, when you have gone to the furthest extent in opposing it and contending against it, and it may well be the truth, so that you have destroyed yourselves? His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿from one who is in extreme opposition﴾ is placed in the position of "you" (منكم), clarifying their condition and description.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 41, verses 53–54:

"We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves" means: what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, facilitated for His Messenger ﷺ and for the caliphs after him, and the helpers of his religion, in the horizons of the world and the lands of the East and West in general, and in the courtyard (bāḥa) of the Arabs [[The phrase "in the courtyard of the Arabs": i.e. their open space (sāḥa). Cited from al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] in particular: of the conquests the like of which was not made easy for any of the caliphs of the earth before them, and of the victories over tyrants and Chosroes, and of making the few prevail over the many, and of empowering the weak over their strong, and of Allah carrying out through their hands matters outside the familiar and beyond ordinary custom, and of the spreading of the call of Islam across the regions of the inhabited world, and the extension of its dominion to its furthest reaches. Inquiry will reveal to you, in the histories and the written books, in the scenes and days of its people, wonders such that no single event of theirs is witnessed except as one of the signs of Allah and one of His verses, by which certainty is strengthened and faith increased, and it becomes clear that the religion of Islam is the religion of truth, from which none turns away except one who is obstinate in his senses and deceives himself. Steadfastness and uprightness are nothing but the attribute of truth and sincerity, just as instability and wavering are the attribute of falsehood and fabrication; and falsehood has a wind that blows and then subsides, and a dominion that appears and then vanishes.

"Is it not sufficient that your Lord" — "your Lord" is in the nominative position, as the subject of "sufficient" (kafā). "That He is over all things a Witness" is a substitute (badal) for it; the intended sense is: "Is it not sufficient for them that your Lord is over all things a Witness?" Its meaning: this promised manifestation of Allah's signs in the horizons and within themselves they will see and witness, and at that time they will realize that the Qur'an is a revelation from the One who knows the unseen, who is over all things a Witness, that is, an all-observing Guardian for whom His unseen and His seen are alike. This suffices them as proof that it is true and that it is from Him. Had it not been so, it would not have gained this strength, nor would its bearers have been given this victory. It is also read "fī mirya" (in doubt) with a ḍamma, and mirya means doubt.

"Surely He is All-Encompassing (muḥīṭ)": knowing, comprehending things with their details, their outward and inward aspects, so that nothing of them is hidden from Him, and He will requite them for their disbelief and their doubt concerning the meeting with their Lord.

Inquiry will reveal to you, in the histories and the written books, in the scenes and days of its people, wonders such that no single event of theirs is witnessed except as one of the signs of Allah and one of His verses, by which certainty is strengthened and faith increased, and it becomes clear that the religion of Islam is the religion of truth, from which none turns away except one who is obstinate in his senses and deceives himself. Steadfastness and uprightness are nothing but the attribute of truth and sincerity, just as instability and wavering are the attribute of falsehood and fabrication; and falsehood has a wind that blows and then subsides, and a dominion that appears and then vanishes.

"Is it not sufficient that your Lord" — "your Lord" is in the nominative position, as the subject of "sufficient" (kafā). "That He is over all things a Witness" is a substitute (badal) for it; the intended sense is: "Is it not sufficient for them that your Lord is over all things a Witness?" Its meaning: this promised manifestation of Allah's signs in the horizons and within themselves they will see and witness, and at that time they will realize that the Qur'an is a revelation from the One who knows the unseen, who is over all things a Witness, that is, an all-observing Guardian for whom His unseen and His seen are alike. This suffices them as proof that it is true and that it is from Him. Had it not been so, it would not have gained this strength, nor would its bearers have been given this victory. It is also read "fī mirya" (in doubt) with a ḍamma, and mirya means doubt.

"Surely He is All-Encompassing (muḥīṭ)": knowing, comprehending things with their details, their outward and inward aspects, so that nothing of them is hidden from Him, and He will requite them for their disbelief and their doubt concerning the meeting with their Lord.

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Sajda, Allah will give him ten good deeds for every letter."
